messages:
Rachel: Heads-up — we need a quick decision on how we propagate customer CAs to the private control plane over per-customer peering. Options on the table: central vault fetch, push-to-relay sidecars, or rely on AWS Private CA cross-account trust. Tradeoffs?

Kevin: Short thoughts: central fetch = single source of truth + easy audit but becomes a perf/hotspot & single point for rotation. Push-to-relay isolates blast radius but adds deployment/upgrade complexity. AWS Private CA avoids us managing keys but is a vendor lock and has cross-account UX.

Sandeep: Also note chain size implications. Long chains + OCSP stapling can blow initial TLS handshake size and flakily fail on some NATs. We saw issues with ~1.2KB chains in earlier tests. Worth modelling MTU fragmentation.

Ola: +1 for auditability. If we push certs to relays we need signed metadata/versioning so we don't lose track of what is active where. Otherwise ops becomes a guessing game.

Rachel: Route53 / DNS surface is another cost angle. If we do per-customer namespacing like cp.{cust}.private.redwood, that implies many record sets or lots of hosted zones. That scales poorly cost-wise. Ideas to avoid per-customer hosted zones?

Kevin: Could we use a single hosted zone and create many records? Possibly, but record-count limits and request cost still scale. Wildcard certs across tenants is tempting but kills strong isolation. SAN-heavy certs are brittle and size-limited.

Sandeep: A different pattern: publish a signed manifest from the central control plane that describes the customer cert metadata (version, SHA256, expiry, cert_url). Relays fetch the manifest, verify signature against Redwood root key, then fetch the cert only when needed. That reduces push traffic and keeps a central source of truth.

Carol: Manifest idea sounds good. Bootstrapping is the trick: relays need a trust anchor when they first come up. Use existing agent bootstrap flow to give a short-lived provisioning token and the Redwood root signing cert during install. After that, manifests handle rotation.

infra-bot: cert-rotation job queued for customer-688 at 2026-03-19T21:10:23Z (job-id: rot-688-20260319).

Rachel: Good. Operationally we also need fallback semantics: relays should continue serving last-known cert if manifest fetch fails (with alerts). We can't hard-break when peering briefly flaps.

Kevin: Agreed. Playbook idea: generate new cert -> publish signed manifest -> relays fetch+verify -> reload -> monitor -> deprecate old cert after X. Need X chosen and an emergency rollback path.

Sandeep: I can add MTU/NAT test vectors to the RFC to ensure handshake size is safe on common provider NATs and CF/LB setups. Also include perf numbers on manifest fetch rates to estimate vault load.

Rachel: Proposal: adopt manifest-signed propagation + agent bootstrap trust anchor. Default deprecation window X = 24h, customer-configurable. Rollback if error rate >5% in 15m post-rotation. Ops notified by trace alerts.

Carol: PoC snippet for manifest verification: 

```
# pseudo
manifest = fetch("https://cp.internal/manifest/customer-688")
if verify_signature(manifest, redwood_root_pub):
    cert = fetch(manifest.cert_url)
    if sha256(cert) == manifest.cert_sha256:
        install(cert)
```

Kevin: I'll draft an RFC titled "manifest-signed cert propagation + bootstrap trust anchor" and include test plan. @Sandeep can you attach MTU/NAT test results?

Sandeep: On it — I'll run NAT50/CloudFront/LB vectors and post results in the RFC thread.

Rachel: Ops owners: Kevin -> RFC & rollouts, Carol -> prototype, Sandeep -> test vectors. Thanks all :thumbsup:

Kevin: Filing RFC today.
